To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the residual-gas damping coefficient of a torsion pendulum in a nearby housing increases significantly when the distance to the surrounding walls is comparable to or smaller than the test masses themselves.
residual-gas damping and the associated force noise increase when the distance between a test mass and the surrounding housing is smaller than the size of the test mass.

the damping coefficient, and therefore the thermal noise, of a test mass increases by a factor 1.5-2.3, depending on test mass geometry, if the distance between the mass and its housing is smaller than the size of the mass.

the residual-gas damping force acting on a macroscopic object in the molecular flow limit, which is a limiting factor in many small-force experiments.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the residual gas damping coefficient of a test mass in the molecular flow is not only proportional to the pressure, as expected, but also to the inverse of the test mass volume.
, for a macroscopic body in the molecular flow limit, there is an increased residual gas force noise when the body is enclosed in a volume with a size comparable to the body.
the effect of the housing on the damping coefficient is not a simple one, but rather a complex one, which is a function of the housing geometry and the distance between the housing and the test mass.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the residual-gas thermal force noise is not negligible and can be a limiting factor in the sensitivity of future gravitational wave observatories.

the residual-gas damping is not only a function of gas pressure, temperature, and test-mass size but also a function of test-mass housing size and geometry, which is not accounted for in the current models.
the residual gas force noise is not a negligible noise source for the LISA test masses.
The main takeaway from our work is that
residual-gas damping and thermal force noise in a constrained volume can be significantly higher than in a large volume, which is relevant for a wide variety of experiments in the small-force regime.
the thermal force noise is not a fundamental property of a gas volume but is rather determined by the geometry of the test mass and the gas volume.

residual-gas damping and the associated noise should be taken into account in the design of any force-measuring apparatus in which the test mass is confined in a volume of dimensions comparable to the size of the mass itself, and where the gas pressure is not too small.
